WORDS

OF THE GLORIOUS

SAINT ANNE MOTHER OF THE IMMACULATE

presenting the Rules to her Daughters

PIACENZA

FRANCESCO SOLARI PRINTING HOUSE

My daughter, you know that what must guide a daughter in all her steps is the word of her Mother. Take, then, my daughter, this little book which I present to you. It contains my word, which shows you what I was throughout my whole life, and so makes known to you what you, in imitation of me, must be throughout yours. This word of mine will be the light that guides you, and it will be the strength that moves you in all your doing. But whence, my daughter, does this word of mine take the power to be your guide and your impulse? From this: that my word is the very word of my Immaculate Daughter, it is that of her Son, my Grandson Jesus, it is, in short, that of God himself. Indeed, all that you will read in this little book, all of it is good, all of it leads to the love of your God and of your neighbour; all of it will urge you to flee vice and to practise the virtues; all of it will kindle you to the observance of the evangelical counsels. Now, my daughter, you know well that man can have neither a good word nor a good thought by himself alone. Therefore, my daughter, you are to receive this little book as a work of God, and not as a work of man. In it you will find the thinking, the feeling, the affections, the speaking and the acting of my Grandson Jesus Christ, but inasmuch as all these things have formed my mind, my heart, my affections, my actions and my whole spirit; and therefore they come to you with the features and the lineaments of me, your Mother, so that — by virtue of the spiritual birth you have received from me, already bearing the image of God and my image, and being an adopted daughter of God and my daughter — by observing the word written in this little book, the image of God and my image may grow in you and then be brought to completion, the daughter of God and my daughter may grow in you and then be brought to completion; and so on earth and in Heaven you may be my joy, my delight, my honour and my crown. My daughter, receive, then, this gift of mine with that impetus of burning love with which I, your most loving Mother, present it to you. Know, my daughter, that I cannot show you my love and motherly care in a more lively, more heartfelt and more tender way than by the gift of these my Rules; and so you will not be able to respond to such motherly charity towards you except by consecrating yourself and all your strength to a continual and exact observance of them. Observe them, then, my daughter, and be certain that, by observing them, they will unite you ever more closely to me your Mother, to my Immaculate Daughter, to my Grandson Jesus, to your God; which is as much as to say that they will make you [?] perfect and holy in your vocation, and in the end will lead you to Heaven. May God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit grant you all this through my intercession. Amen.

COMMON RULES

OF THE DAUGHTERS

OF SAINT ANNE MOTHER OF THE IMMACULATE

AND MINIMS

OF SAINT FRANCIS OF ASSISI

End of the Institute. — Members who compose it. — Spirit of the Institute.

No. 1. End of the Institute.

The Holy Mother. — My daughter, the end which my family has in common with all Christians is to imitate Jesus Christ. Jesus is the Holy One by essence, and at the same time he is the one who makes all the saints; and all those who follow him are called to be saints with the holiness of him who is their Head; and moreover they are called to help their neighbours, so that they too may become saints. But besides this vocation common to all Christians, my daughters have one which is proper to them alone; and this vocation is that they imitate Jesus Christ not only in himself, but that they imitate him also in me, their Holy Mother, who am a copy of him and a most luminous picture. Here, then, my daughter, is the special end to which all of you are called, and which distinguishes my Institute from every other Religious Institute.

God calls you to my family so that you may be my imitators; so that you may be most splendid copies of me, the Mother of the Immaculate. This work must be the work of divine Love; but divine Love must carry it so far forward as to imprint me and my spirit in you in such a way that you are not only my devotees, my friends, but are also my daughters; so that I may be wholly in you, and you in me, I may live in you, and you in me; I may see myself in you, and see you in me; and whoever looks at me may see you, and whoever looks at you may see me. Do you see, my daughter, what the rays of the Sun do, which, setting out from that star, go and strike upon a most clear crystal? They paint in it the face of the sun, and make of it another sun in miniature. So it is with you, my daughters: the splendours of my spirit, of my holiness and of my virtues must so strike upon your souls as to form in them most beautiful and most splendid likenesses of me. Have you now clearly understood, then, what the end of your vocation is? God has called you to my family so that you may imitate Jesus Christ in me, your Holy Mother. After this, you are called to make me known and to make me loved by your neighbours, so that, having recourse to me in prayer, they may obtain the grace to become holy. You are like the key to my Heart: you open it, so that those classes of persons whom God will entrust to the care of my Institute may enjoy the treasure of my riches of grace. Now you have learned the whole end of my daughters. The principal end is to attend to their own perfection by imitating me in all my virtues, and so to become saints; and the secondary end is to help others to become holy, exhorting them to place themselves under my special protection. My daughter, if you attain this twofold aim of my family, you will be perfect.

The daughter. — My Mother, what a sublime vocation has fallen to me! I thank you that, without any merit of mine, you asked the Most Holy Trinity to make me your daughter. Happy am I if I attain its end! for then, like ripe fruit, I shall fall back upon your bosom, from which I came forth into the light of so great a grace! Oh, to rest blessed upon your bosom! upon that bosom in which the Immaculate, the divine Mary, was conceived and rested for nine months! Ah! in falling upon your bosom I shall fall upon the bosom of Mary, upon that of Jesus, upon the bosom of my God, to rest there blessed together with you for all Eternity.

2. Members who compose the Institute.

My daughter, what persons of your sex do you think may form part of my family? It is like Noah’s Ark, which saves every kind of person from shipwreck: in it unmarried women and widows, young and old, may find a place, provided that they have no impediments incompatible with the offices of the Institute, provided that they have all those testimonials which make up a good reputation, and provided that they give signs of an unmistakable heavenly vocation. Here are the conditions: 1. I wish them to have the spontaneous consent of their Parents: this is to be understood as the ordinary rule. 2. Ordinarily they will not be received if they have already been members of another Institute; and the same is to be said if they have been in service. 3. When someone presents herself to make the request to be admitted, before any answer is given she is exhorted to make a novena to me, your Holy Mother, and the community of the novitiate house makes it too, and she is asked to return. 4. She is made acquainted in general with the dispositions she must have in order to be admitted, and with the principal obligations of the Institute. 5. As soon as she is admitted as a postulant, she will make five days of spiritual retreat in honour of my five joys, during which she will make a general confession of her whole life to the ordinary confessor of the sisters, or to another who will be assigned to her by the Superior. During the time of these exercises she communicates only with the guardian assigned to her. 6. They must be prepared, once the novitiate is completed, to make the four simple vows of poverty, chastity, obedience, and assistance to the sick. What the matter of these vows is will appear from those chapters where these virtues are treated. 7. These vows are for a year, and when the year is ended they lapse; and those who wish to continue to form part of the Institute must renew them. They must be prepared to make these vows perpetual when the Superiors judge fit. 8. Thus my Institute is composed of members who have simple annual vows and simple perpetual vows. The vows of the Institute, when they are perpetual, carry joined with them the vow of perpetual stability in the Institute. My daughters are all equal: from the Superior down to the last, they have no outward distinction; among them seniority, years of vocation, labours sustained, offices held in the company, must not be distinguished except by greater virtue, e.g. by greater humility, mortification and the like.

3. Spirit of the Institute.

My daughter, you must know that the Holy Spirit wrought in me one of the most beautiful works of his divine grace: in me all the righteousness and all the holiness of the old law found, as it were, their completion; in me the groans, the sighs, the tears and the prayers of all the just of the old testament came to rest, because from me, as from their most fruitful root, there sprang my daughter Mary Immaculate, and Jesus Christ her Son and the Son of God, the source of the new law of love. If, then, you want my spirit, you have only to paint in your mind the most beautiful, the most splendid and the most exact picture of the life of my blessed Daughter and of my Grandson Jesus. This picture you will find in the chapter that follows.

Virtues that compose the Spirit of the Institute. — Actions by which the Spirit of the Institute is acquired and perfected. — Actions by which it is spread to others.

Faith.

The Holy Mother. — My daughter, faith rests upon the word of God. After the Humanity of Jesus Christ, which is personally united to the substantial Word of God, she who most rested upon the word of God was my Immaculate Daughter, who believed the Archangel Gabriel when he announced to her that she would be the Mother of God. And after Mary come I, who believed that in my womb there would be accomplished the work which, after that of the Incarnation, is the most sublime and the furthest from human lights: I mean the Immaculate conception of my daughter Mary. Therefore, to have in you this spirit of mine of living and strong faith, you must fix your spirit firmly on this truth: that the word of God is always true and can never deceive, and so leads infallibly to happiness whoever trusts in it; on the contrary, the word of the devil, of the flesh and of the world is always deceitful, and whoever follows it goes to eternal perdition. Penetrate well what my Grandson Jesus says: that his word is like a building built upon rock, which is not shaken by the furious blast of the winds and the rain; but the word of the world may be compared to a house whose foundations are laid upon the sand, and which, shaken by the winds and the rains, falls in ruin to the ground. Therefore the resolution must be firm in you always to conform your affections and your doing to the teachings of Jesus Christ, and never to those of the world. Pray often to God to enlighten your superiors, so that they may give my daughters confessors who are devoted to the Pope and attached in all and for all to his sentiments. The prayer which I shall receive willingly will be the one you make to me so that I may obtain for your confessors a filial and boundless devotion to the Head of the Church, and that the whole world may be enlightened by the holy faith.

Virtue of Hope.

My daughter, do you know how I prepared myself to become the mother of her who was, as it were, the gate of the Kingdom of God? Because those words of Jesus Christ which say, “Seek first of all the Kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all other things shall be added unto you,” were well engraved in my mind and in my heart, and were practised by me even before my Jesus had preached them. Know, O my daughter, that Jesus Christ, and his grace, and the glory of God, and the salvation of the soul — which are precisely the things that form the Kingdom of God — and the practice of virtue and the observance of the divine commandments, which form its righteousness, were always my treasure, to which my heart and my longings continually went.

This spirit of hope of mine, my daughter, must be yours too. To possess it, then, do as follows: 1. Persuade yourself well that Jesus, his grace, the glory of your God, the salvation of your soul are such goods that they alone suffice to make you eternally blessed, and that every other good different from these would neither suffice you nor is necessary for your eternal happiness; likewise be firmly persuaded that the practice of virtue, the flight from vice, the observance of the divine commandments and of all your duties are the straight road to lead you to the Kingdom of God. 2. Live without anxiety as regards earthly goods and bodily health, leaving to God the care of all these things. 3. Say often with the Holy Apostle: I would rather suffer hunger, thirst, infamy, torments, and death itself, than offend my God, than detach myself even for a little from the love of my Jesus, than fail in anything in my duties. 4. Form a firm persuasion that, when you are well planted in this heavenly hope, you will always live like a little child in the arms of your heavenly Father, so that you will never lack anything that would be truly good for you, and no evil will ever befall you; and this will be so even if at some moment it should seem to you, and seem to others too, that everything was lost to you.

Virtue of Charity.

Do you know, beloved of my heart, whither Faith and hope are directed? Are you instructed on this point, so very important? Listen well: faith and hope aspire to charity, which is, as it were, the soul and the life of them both. Do you see the human body? It needs to have the soul, and without it, it is a piece of dead earth, and cannot last long without turning to dust: so it is with Faith and Hope: they need to be informed and quickened by Charity, because without it they are as dead; they have no beauty, and cannot last without corrupting. Indeed, see, my daughter, the damned: because Charity is impossible for them, so they can have neither faith nor hope. My dear daughter, Charity aflame with the pure love of God was truly that heavenly fire which made my womb fruitful, so that I might worthily conceive, with an immaculate conception, my daughter Mary. But the love of compassion for the poor children of Adam, the sighs for the coming of the Redeemer, the tears and the prayers to hasten it, watered it so as to furnish most pure matter for that conception. But do you wish, then, to know what the Charity of God and of neighbour is like? This Jesus Christ has taught us with those words of his which say: “The things that please my Father, I do always.” From these words it appears clearly that the pure love of God consists in this: that our pleasure should always and solely come to rest in the pleasure of our God. When the pleasure of our heavenly Father is the only thing and the only Treasure of your heart, then it is, my daughter, that you will truly love him with pure love. For do you not know, my daughter, that what makes our heavenly Father happy and blessed is his own pleasure? He is blessed because he has in himself a supreme pleasure; when, then, you place all your delight in the pleasure of your God, then it means that the one thing that pleases you is to know that your heavenly Father is content and happy, is blessed: and this means to love him with the love of charity, with pure love, with filial love, with a love worthy of him, worthy of being in his company for all eternity. My daughter, the pleasure which you take in the pleasure of your God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, when it is perfect and consummated, will then also be your beatitude; for what endowment of yours do you think can make you blessed? Surely that which draws upon you the eyes of your God. Now the delight which you take in his divine pleasure is precisely the endowment of yours which most enamours him of you; and therefore it is also your true supreme good, it is your true happiness. But as what your God most loves in you is that eagerness to procure him every pleasure, so this same thing is what he most loves in your neighbours; and therefore you will love these neighbours of yours with most pure Charity when you will and procure for them that they set their heart on seeking in everything and always the delight of the heavenly Father.

The daughter. — Dearest Mother, my glorious Saint Anne, you have set in my heart most ardent longings to delight my God. Tell me, then, the road to reach it.

The Holy Mother. — My daughter, you will give testimony that your heart seeks nothing but the pleasure of your Lord if you do those things which he most wants from you. Now: 1. he most wants from you those things which your superiors and your holy Rules want; 2. between the things that flatter the flesh and those that vex it, he wants the second more than the first; 3. those things which please nature and which at the same time your God wills, move yourself towards them not for the motive that they give delight, but because in them, as in flowers, you can gather for yourself [gather there] the honey of the divine will; 4. in any occurrence that comes upon you unexpectedly, whether it refreshes the soul and the body, or saddens the one or the other, or even both, bless the hand of your Lord from which it is sent to you; 5. and keep all this conduct of yours in order to imitate Jesus Christ, who always kept it. Here, my daughter, is the sure road to live by the sole pleasure of your God, and to love him perfectly.

Virtue of simplicity.

My daughter, our God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is most simple: there can be no duplicity in him, so that in him thinking, speaking, will, affections, doing, all is in full accord, and he has no composition. I, my daughter, perfectly imitated this perfection of the heavenly Father: in me everything was in perfect harmony; all my words were a mirror of my thought; whoever heard how I spoke knew also how I thought; my intentions were in full accord with my mind; my will, my affections, my works were expressions of my aims [?]; all my exterior was in conformity with my spirit; and my whole person, finally, was a copy perfectly submissive and conformed to my God. I was truly that single eye of the gospel which, gazing fixedly at the eternal sun of justice, was full of light, and made my whole life shine with light. Thus in me was fulfilled the word of Jesus Christ, namely that God is pleased to reveal his secrets to the simple, and keeps them hidden from the wise of the world. For to me was revealed one of his most hidden counsels, I mean that of the Immaculate conception of Mary, to be accomplished in my womb, and her destiny to become the Mother of God. My daughter, in imitation of me, see to it that in you there be nothing of duplicity: let all in you be light, so that your words may be like rays which reveal to all, above all to your superiors, everything that passes through your mind; and in all your works aim at nothing but your true treasure, which is the pleasure of your God; and then he will willingly converse intimately with you.

Virtue of Prudence.

My daughter, simplicity cannot live without the company of prudence; for without it, it degenerates into insipidity and clumsiness. Prudence is that light which, between two things, always makes you choose the one that better leads you to acquire and to increase the only solid wealth, that is, the love of God; it is that which, between two words, prefers the one that is to the praise of God, and leaves aside the one that would be lacking in reverence to him; it chooses the one that honours one’s neighbour, and leaves the one that would harm him; the one that can be an exercise of humility, and rejects the one that would bend it towards vanity; it keeps silent or speaks according as the one or the other leads straight to divine Love. So it is with doing: it always discerns what is more for the glory of God and the good of one’s neighbour. Moreover, in all its judgements it never takes its rule either from what the world thinks or even from human reasoning, but Jesus Christ is its master in everything. My daughter, prudence in these parts of it enumerated so far was so much with me that it made me worthy to give birth to Her who is the most prudent Virgin. Follow me, and so you will be simple as the dove and prudent as the serpent. To be prudent in this way, be careful to keep far from you the prudence of the flesh and of the devil, which always seeks: 1. what can make it appear before men, and be esteemed, loved and honoured by them; 2. it claims to dominate everyone, and would have everyone subject to its way of seeing and to its will, so that no one sees rightly unless with its eyes, no one wills rightly unless he wills what it wills; 3. it chooses what can procure it sensual comforts, and cares nothing either for the glory of God or for the salvation of its neighbours. Flee, for charity’s sake, this prudence, which is wholly diabolical.

Virtue of humility

My daughter, you see me placed by God upon the Throne of the most high dignity of Mother of his own divine mother: a singular dignity, and one which I share with no other Woman. This means, then, that I was, after Mary, the most humble among creatures, humility being the road to the exaltation that comes from God. My daughter, learn well to know what humility is. Humility, then, is a sincere confession, a confession made with love, that the creature has before God no merit to be sanctified, has no merit to have the grace of doing good and fleeing evil, has no merit to have qualities and gifts that raise it above others, and that, if it is adorned with them, it has no right to use them to look upon its neighbours with an indifferent and contemptuous eye; rather it must use them for the good of others; finally, it has no merit to be predestined to eternal happiness. Nor is this enough; but the truly humble person, in the present condition of nature, relishes and loves to confess that he is a sinner and is proud; and therefore in his own eyes he abases himself and esteems himself most contemptible; and he loves others to regard him as a sinner and proud, and to take from this knowledge a reason for despising him. The humble person loves to confess that even from the gifts received from God, from his good works, above all if they are done under the eyes of others, he may run the danger of growing vain; hence he does everything to keep his heavenly treasure hidden; and all the good he does to his neighbour (and he strives to do much) he uses every device so that it may pass unobserved; and if sometimes he does not succeed in this and receives some praise for it, then he attributes everything to the divine goodness, which, moved by the prayers and merits of good people, has favoured him. Now have you seen, my daughter, what face holy humility has? The humble person, my daughter, carries deeply engraved in the soul those words of Jesus Christ which say: “Whoever among you wishes to be the greatest, let him make himself the least and the servant of all.” The humble woman, armed with these divine words, overcomes the vice of ambition; a vice which drives one to covet the posts that seem honourable, to desire, e.g., to be made superior, vice-superior, and so on; and when the ambitious woman is not satisfied in these most wicked longings of hers, then she is moved to murmur against the superiors because they prefer others to her, and she charges them with being persons of little discernment in recognising merit and capacity for offices; and she goes even further, charging them with being respecters of persons and with having aims of their own interest in the elections they make to fill the posts; she is moved also to envy towards those who are placed in them, and accuses them of having procured the post by their intrigues, by their hypocrisy and by their flattery of the Superiors. If, then, the ambitious woman manages to obtain the office of Superior, she seeks nothing from that office but her own comforts, she seeks only to be honoured by her fellow sisters, whom she regards as so many slaves of hers: woe if any of them, even through inadvertence, fails in the slightest in reverence towards her: she leaves her no more peace; she persecutes her and makes her suffer in every way; she looks at her with a sullen and contemptuous eye; if the poor thing approaches her with some request, she speaks to her ungraciously, or worse, turns her back on her and gives her no answer. Of every evil that happens in the community the unfortunate one is always the culprit! These ambitious women, once placed in office, do not think at all of discharging its duties; they let observance decline, and so they damn themselves and are the ruin of the Institute.

My daughter, I want you to know that this vice of ambition is one of those vices that, if anyone were tainted with it and, when corrected by the Superiors, did not amend, she must be inexorably sent away from my Institute. My daughter, set well in your heart the words of Jesus Christ quoted above, so as to keep far from this vice. Bend your eye upon yourself, and see a little whether this ugly vice of ambition has perhaps crept in some way into your soul, and at once put it out with an act of deep humility, by which in your own eyes you lower yourself, abase yourself, and annihilate yourself beneath the feet of all your sisters. To drive it from your heart, have yourself helped by your superior, opening yourself to her candidly. And if ever the distinguished place you occupy should be what tempts you to ambition, then do as follows: make known to your Superiors that that place gives you temptation to ambition and vanity, and that, for charity’s sake, they should take it from you if they please, putting you in whatever more obscure place they wish. My daughter, humility must make you ready to receive with a good heart all occasions of humbling yourself: if, e.g., at some time, whether often or seldom, your Superior admonishes you and corrects you for some fault of yours, in private or before all the sisters, kneel down at once and listen willingly to the admonition, and then, as a sign that you have welcomed it, humbly kiss the ground. Likewise in chapter, confess your fault, moved by a true spirit of humility. Moreover, be glad, and intend to give full right, that any one of your sisters who observes in you even the least fault, even one committed only once, should go at once, without your knowing, to make it known to your Superior, so that with her counsels and her penances you may soon obtain pardon for it, and the grace not to commit it again. And even if the thing in question did not seem to you a fault, or you were altogether innocent of it, you will not for that reason complain; rather you are to rejoice that thus you are like Jesus Christ, who was so greatly humiliated without any fault of his own; and in this case think also that that correction and that penance for a fault not committed by you will be good for atoning for so many others that you will have committed. My daughter, attend to this last act of humility, since it is very important that you make every effort to be full of it; for do you know what evil befalls those who lack it? They are always in suspicion that this one or that one is reporting their faults to the Superior; and when it seems to them that they can fix this suspicion of theirs upon some sister in particular, then at once they take offence, and conceive against her a certain aversion, look at her with a suspicious eye, and give her the shameful name of the Superior’s spy. These unfortunate ones, when they abandon themselves to this spirit of pride, are truly wretched, and buried in the malice of Lucifer. My daughter, these sentiments of humility which you have regarding your own person, you must have also regarding your whole Institute. So listen to the humble sentiments I want you to nourish towards it. 1. You must be convinced and persuaded that your Institute is the last of all those that adorn the Church, that it is faulty, and has little grace in discharging the offices entrusted to it by Providence. 2. You will indeed pray that your Institute may be faithful to God in its duties; but you will not long for it to spread into many places. 3. With outsiders you will never speak of it with praise; and when you speak of it among yourselves, you will use no other name than that of Poor Institute, or our poor Company. 4. You will take good care not to show to any person, of whatever condition, under whatever pretext, whether of friendship or of kinship, a desire that she should embrace your Institute and become a Religious in it. 5. The superiors will take care that nothing be written in praise of the Institute and its functions. 6. You will take care not to desire that the good which the Institute does be placed under the eyes of men; rather you must sincerely long that no account be taken of your Institute, that no good opinion be held of it, but rather that it be forgotten and despised by all, and spoken ill of. And when you hear that some city is asking for the foundation of some house of yours, you, astonished, will raise your eyes to heaven and say: O Lord, how is it possible that you should wish to make use of beings and persons as faulty as we are for your works? Ah! Lord, I cannot explain this mystery otherwise than by thinking that you set your eyes upon us precisely because you see us to be the most useless of beings, so that all the glory may be yours and not the creature’s. 7. Yet, notwithstanding this low esteem which you must have of the Institute, the love you bear it will be immense, most tender, strong, and preferred above every other Institute, considering that God has made you to be born in it and of it, and that it is your mother, which has given you that most noble being and that fortunate name of my daughter; now you know well that one does not choose one’s Mother, but she is given by God; and the love one feels towards one’s Mother does not arise from her qualities of being, e.g., rich, beautiful, a Queen, esteemed by all; no, no; but it arises precisely from her being our Mother, that is, the one whom God has taken as his companion in giving us the life we have and in bringing us into the world. See, my daughter, that Baby, how he nestles at his mamma’s breast, even though she is a poor peasant woman, ugly and poorly dressed? How he finds there all his joys, how he rests there with a continual smile on his lips? He does not deign even a glance at any other woman, however noble and rich. So it must be with you: God has willed you to be born in my family; this is enough for you to love it above any other, for you to find in its bosom all your joys and happiness, and for whoever sees you in it to see you always with a serene face and a smile on your lips. And if you are asked: Are you content in this Institute? answer at once: And why not? Ought I not to be content and blessed in the family in which God has made me to be born? My daughter, here I have given you sublime lessons on humility: I have told you about it what I always practised in my life. It was always my favourite virtue; it was the foundation of all my other virtues; it was the golden knot that gathered them all into a most beautiful body; it was that which brought them to that high point which merited for me to give to the world the Immaculate mother of God; it was, finally, that which set upon my head that crown of glory which I shall enjoy for all eternity. Blessed are you, my daughter, if you imitate me in this virtue! With it you will always be in peace and in joy. But woe to those among my daughters who should lack it! Without it they would be stripped of what little good they might have, and they would be continually in agitation, in anguish and in ill humour.

Virtue of meekness.

The Holy Mother. — Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth: this, my daughter, is a saying of my Jesus. Listen to me attentively: human nature, in the person of woman, is that earth which was created by God so that it might bring forth for him fruits of blessing. But, to speak rightly, I was the only one among women to obtain this blessing, because I was the only one who from my womb brought forth Her who was the only Immaculate one; and therefore my flesh was truly holy ground, blessed ground. You see, then, that I, above every mortal, was Mistress of the earth; and therefore above all others I had the beatitude promised to the meek; say, indeed, that I was the gentlest among the children of God. But was not Mary also the true earth, the new earth, which from her flesh, by the sole power of the Holy Spirit, brought forth Jesus Christ, who is the fruit of the true knowledge of good and evil, who is the fruit of every delight to the palate and of every beauty to the eyes? Now Mary was a wealth of mine; and therefore, if I merited her from the Father of the family, it was because I made him the offering of a meekness unequalled by any meek person. Therefore you would not be a worthy daughter of mine, if you were not very distinguished in this virtue, and did not go ahead of other religious persons. My daughters are called to possess the earth of the hearts of men, to cultivate them, so that they may yield those fruits for which they are created, that is, the fruits of divine love and of all the other Christian virtues. And what are all the compassionate cares which you give to the sick in the hospitals and in private houses? Are they not a most powerful cultivation, which effectively awakens them to recognise the goodness, the mercy, the providence of the heavenly Father, and to give themselves wholly to him through a sincere conversion? Say the same of your cares for the poor girls in danger. You are the lambs filled with the virtue of the Lamb of God, who, consuming your flesh for the sake of the wolves, and being, so to speak, eaten by them, convert them too into lambs of God. Therefore, my daughter, consecrate yourself wholly to this virtue, and be to all your neighbours sweet as honey, if you wish to be wholly mine, and in the end to possess, in my company, the land of holy Paradise. Here, so far, I have taught you those virtues which formed my spirit; a spirit always steadfast in me, a spirit that informed my whole life, all my steps. All my doing was animated by living faith, firm hope, ardent charity, dovelike simplicity, enlightened prudence, deep humility and meekness. And if you are my daughter, in begetting you I can give you no other life than the spirit of these virtues, which is my very life. And whoever among you did not possess it would bear the name of my daughter, but would not be so in reality. And so noble a name would be for her nothing but confusion and eternal ignominy.

2. Actions by which the Spirit of the Institute is acquired, and actions by which it is spread to others.

You know, my beloved daughter, that the spirit is what makes us live and makes us move: all our works are like fruits that spring from the tree of our spirit. But precisely because they spring from our spirit, so they must return to it and be gathered up in it; which is as much as to say that our actions must serve to increase our spirit until it comes to be ripe, so as to be placed in the heavenly Homeland. But besides the actions which serve you, my daughter, to perfect in you this spirit of mine of which I am speaking to you, there are those works by which you strive to spread it among your neighbours, to help them to become holy. The first are the principal ones, because they serve to make you yourself holy, and the others are secondary, and serve you to sanctify others. The first actions are of two kinds: some help you to detach yourself from creatures, so as to unite yourself wholly to your God; and others unite you immediately to your God, and to your neighbour as the image of God. Of all these actions I shall speak to you in the following chapters.

Evangelical Poverty, of which the Daughters of Saint Anne make a vow

The Holy Mother. — 1. My daughter, to understand how moderate in me were the love of the goods of the earth and the use of them, observe how I merited that my goods should serve to nourish the Mother of God, who honoured them, so to speak, by using them with the highest order, with the highest virtue and merit; I merited that they should then serve for the sustenance of the very Son of God, who, by using them, sanctified them in such a way that afterwards he made them the matter of the Sacraments, which sanctify the world. You may be sure, then, that no one surpassed me in that detachment from possessions which my Grandson Jesus showed, who, although Master of everything, yet would not have a stone on which to rest his head. You are called to imitate this virtue of Jesus and of mine by making a vow of it. Listen, then, from me, what the poverty is of which you make a vow in the Institute: first as regards the goods of the Institute itself, and then as regards those of your family.

  1. Know first that my Institute, since it must procure assistance for the poor sick and maintain the girls in danger, may possess immovable and movable goods of every kind. But these goods are the common goods of all my dear daughters who compose my Institute, and are not the goods of any one in particular: it is the Institute that possesses, with that possession which the Church grants to Religious Bodies; but the individual Religious person does not possess. This being so, here, then, my daughter, is the Poverty of which you make a vow in my Institute: you make a vow to receive from the hands of your superiors all of those goods that is to serve for your use; so that the reason why you have with you for your use any thing whatever of those goods is because the superiors have assigned it to you; and, asking yourself why you have with you this or that item, you may answer yourself: I have it because my superiors have assigned it to me; asking yourself again why you continue to keep it, and for how long you will continue to keep it, you may answer yourself: because my superiors still leave it to me, and I shall keep it until the moment they ask me for it. In short, the vow of your poverty obliges you not to dispose of the goods of the Institute, either to your own advantage or to the advantage of others, either in great quantity or in the very smallest quantity, without the express permission of the superiors, and in the form in which such permission is given. If you, my daughter, did otherwise, you would commit a sin against your vow of Poverty, either venial or mortal according to the gravity of the matter. From this follow the precepts I give you on Poverty; by observing them you will guard its vow well.

  2. Of the things that are held in common in the community — food, clothes, books, and so with everything — you may take nothing without the permission of your superior; otherwise it would not be true that you have everything from the hands of your superiors. The same is to be said of any thing that has been abandoned or lost: if it comes into your hands, your obligation is to take it to the Superior, were it even a needle.

  3. The things given you by the superiors for your use you may not regard as though they were your own. Hence, in speaking of them, you will not say “my thing,” but “our thing”; our room, our scissors, and so on; otherwise it would not be true that you hold everything at every moment in dependence on the will of your superiors.

  4. You must have nothing, not even a sheet of paper, which you are not ready to give up at any moment and at the least sign from your superiors; otherwise it would not be true that you have everything in dependence on your superiors.

  5. Of all that you have for your use, you may neither give, nor lend, nor exchange anything with any of your sisters without the permission of your superiors; otherwise it would not be true that you hold everything at every moment in dependence on your superiors.

  6. You must be most careful that nothing of what is given for your use, or in any way entrusted to your keeping, be lost, or perish, or be spoiled, or wear out, or grow old through your negligence; otherwise it would not be true that at every moment you must be ready to render an account of it to your superiors. And if you should lose a thing, even a small one, e.g. a key, a pair of scissors, a needle, you will inform the superior of it at once. Likewise you will take care not to write your name on what is given you to use — clothes, books, and anything whatever — because this would reveal in you a sense of ownership. The superiors may indeed mark with your name the things they give you for use; but you may not do so without a failing in poverty.

  7. You are not permitted to keep anything locked up, not even your room with a private key, without the permission of the Superior; for to do otherwise would reveal in you an attachment to ownership. Likewise you must keep nothing hidden from your superiors; otherwise it would not be true that you have everything from the hands of your superiors.

  8. When obedience sends you from one house to another, of what you have for your use you may take nothing without the permission of your superiors.

  9. In the spirit of poverty you will long for the superiors to give you for your use the poorest things of the house, such as the oldest and most patched clothes.

  10. You may not receive anything from the sisters, whether as a gift, or as a loan, or in exchange, without the permission of the Superior.

  11. You are not permitted either to take or to use, even once, what has been given by the superiors for the use of another, were it even an apron, a little lamp, etc., without the permission of those superiors. And if you should find a lost thing, even of little value, e.g. a needle, a thimble, you will take it at once to the Superior.

  12. Once every three months the Superior makes the visitation of the rooms, to see whether my daughters have anything contrary to holy Poverty. On this occasion she will exchange the objects of devotion — little books, holy pictures, small framed pictures, etc. — making them pass from one sister to another, so that they may not become attached to anything.

  13. By virtue of your vow of poverty, you, my daughter, do not give up the ownership of the goods of your family that come to you by any title whatever; you do not cease to be capable of acquiring, by inheritance or in any other way permitted by the laws, any sort of immovable or movable goods.

  14. Of all these goods of which you are the owner, by virtue of your vow of poverty you may not dispose, either by donation, or by contract, or by will, or in any other way permitted by the laws, without the permission of your superiors.

  15. Your vow of poverty leaves you the owner of the revenues of your goods.

  16. Your vow of poverty forbids you to dispose of the revenues of your goods, whether by giving them to relatives, or by making new acquisitions with them, or by using them in almsgiving, or in any other way, without the permission of your superiors.

  17. In whatever way and in whatever measure the goods of your family come into your hands, you, my daughter, by virtue of the vow of poverty, are obliged to place them at once in the hands of your superiors, so that they may become the Institute’s; for none of my daughters, in my family, may possess anything, anything at all.

  18. My daughter, by virtue of the vow of Poverty which you make in my Institute, I do not oblige you, but I do counsel you, that the revenues of your goods — when your relatives have no need of them, and when your superiors give you permission — you yield to your Institute, so that the superiors may use them for the glory of God as they think best. I say the same to you of any sum of money you may acquire.

  19. A daughter of mine who did not persevere in my Institute, but for whatever reason left it, will have no right to claim in justice anything from it, because whatever she had given to my Institute she gave either by virtue of her vow of Poverty, or by a spontaneous and irrevocable donation of her own.

My daughter, all these are the laws of the Poverty of my Institute: blessed are you, and blessed all my daughters who will be faithful in observing them! Freed in this way from the greed for earthly goods, which ruins a great part of the world, they will have taken a great step towards the acquisition of my spirit and of my holiness; for, not considering the things of the earth as goods, they will have a living faith in the eternal goods; and, not caring for earthly things, they will set their heart on hoping for the invisible goods; and, detached from them, they will be able to gather all their love into their God, and they will have no temptations to tell lies for love of them; and so they will be simple; they will use every means to attain divine love, and its fullness in the blessed life; and so they will be prudent; having despised riches, they will have closed a wide door to pride; finally, they will be meek.

The Daughter — My most loving Mother, teach me a way that will lead me briefly and easily to the acquisition of Poverty.

The Holy Mother — Dear one of my heart, here is the road you seek of me: hold firmly to this maxim, to ask for nothing and to refuse nothing of the goods that are necessary to you, such as food, clothing, room, bed, etc., but receive in silence what your superiors give you for your use. It may very well happen at some time that something seems necessary to you, so that you cannot do without it, or seems so harmful to you that you cannot bear it; and in this case you will place yourself at the feet of Christ the Poor One, and of me, your Holy Mother; and if you are enlightened that the matter truly is as it seems to you, then: 1. you will set your soul in a holy indifference to receive from your superiors a yes as well as a no; and thus disposed you will lay the matter before them; and 2. you will be persuaded that in their answer, affirmative or negative, the will of God will be made manifest to you, and you will remain at peace.

Chastity, of which the Daughters of Saint Anne make a vow.

  1. My daughter, to be persuaded that my purity of spirit and of body had no equal, it is enough for you to look at what I was destined for: I mean to conceive the Immaculate Mary, the most pure Mary, the Virgin and Mother, the Mother of God. That love of Purity of my Grandson Jesus, by which he willed to be conceived by the sole power of the Holy Spirit, by which he would not permit his fiercest enemies to form the slightest evil suspicion against his divine purity, although on the other hand he had permitted them to slander him with every crime — this love, I say, of my Jesus found no heart in which it burned more brightly than it did in mine. My daughter, what this vow of Chastity obliges you to is evident: you need only the means to be so faithful to it, to be so pure, as to be worthy to bear the name of my daughter, and hence the name of Sister of my Immaculate Mary. Here they are:

  2. My daughter, this vow consecrates your interior powers of imagination, of fancy, of memory, so that they may harbour no other figure and no other likeness than that of the most sacred humanity of Jesus, than that of Mary, and of me, your Holy Mother, and of the other Saints. And if Satan, against all your efforts and by violence, should paint some earthly face there, you will protest against such violence by invoking the divine help and my help.

  3. Keep the exterior senses in check: the eyes, that they do not rest upon strangers’ faces; the hearing, that it does not receive indecent words; the palate, by not letting it eat or drink outside the appointed times — at least not doing so without the permission of your Superior — by not eating any foods but those which the Community provides, and by drinking water, or a little wine, but very much watered. Touch, by not touching or caressing children without necessity; by not touching animals; take care not to give it more rest [?] than the superiors allow it; in the morning rise from bed most promptly, as soon as you hear the voice of obedience. Never be idle, for idleness is deadly to purity; be always usefully occupied; mortify the sense of smell: this sense too is a great enemy of purity.

  4. When you are obliged by your duty to speak or write to persons of the other sex, of whatever condition they may be, of whatever virtue, whatever bond of kinship they may have with you, take care never to use tender words, or words of too much affection, even if they were pious words. Take good care never to speak with such persons at times and in places not appointed by your superiors. When you speak to them, be careful not to let them come too close to you. Finally, do not presume upon your chastity, as if you were strong enough not to have to fear dangers.

  5. When obedience places you in the assistance of the sick, whether in private houses or in hospitals, you will have a holy fear of the healthy, above all of physicians, surgeons, attendants, and all persons of the other sex employed in and frequenting the hospitals. With them you will deal with that caution with which the apothecary deals with vipers when he extracts the ointment from them; that is, you will deal with them only out of the necessity of having the medicines and what is needed for your sick. When you must speak face to face with these persons, you will do so in an open place and accompanied. In these conversations you will take care not to have on your lips an affected smile, or a look that is too free and worldly; you will not spend unnecessary words; you will not allow them to touch you even with a finger; and if they should attempt this, you will repel them, with a face aflame with indignation, at any cost. Ask often in your prayers for the Holy Spirit’s gift of fortitude, so that in these circumstances you may be a creature above the human, wholly heavenly and without human respect, and ready rather to die than to suffer the least offence to the lily of your purity.

  6. My daughter, if you should see one of your fellow sisters who, in dealing with persons of the other sex — physicians, surgeons, attendants, etc. — was too free, if you saw her chattering with them, etc., and still more if you had grounds to think that she was seized by some affection for anyone, in all these cases you would be obliged to inform the superiors, so that they may remedy it. And woe to you if, through a misconceived charity or under any pretext, you failed to do so, for you would be responsible before God for all the harm of that imprudent one, and for the infamy to which the whole society of my daughters might become subject.

  7. My daughter, if obedience sets you to teach school, take good care not to form a sensible affection for any of your pupils; likewise, do not be easy in letting yourself be touched, embraced, kissed, etc. With them you must have the bearing of a Christian mother, that is, gentle, affable, but mingled with that gravity which draws forth love and reverence.

  8. My daughter, since your vocation puts you in contact with persons of both sexes, it asks of you a purity so white and luminous that with its rays it may enlighten you and all your sisters, in such a way that no eye, however malicious, may harbour suspicion of any of you; a suspicion which, although without any foundation, would nonetheless spread disgrace upon my daughter. Therefore there is no vigilance that ought not to be used by the superiors to keep it far away.

On the Virtue of modesty.

  1. My daughter, modesty is like the veil that serves to guard your chastity. It hides it from the eyes of the profane. Modesty has for its office to place decency and composure in all the outward movements of the body; so that it may appear to those who behold the person that the soul which dwells in it, and is its mistress and governs it, is a holy, pure and angelic soul. My daughter, if my outward bearing had not been adorned with a truly heavenly modesty, I would not have been a worthy temple of the Mother of holy modesty. My daughter, since your life is occupied with your neighbour, holy modesty must take for you the place of an enclosure and of a grille, so that the breath of the world may not offend your purity. Pray your Bridegroom Jesus to make your face, your words and your bearing radiant with the light of His divine modesty, which so drew the crowds towards Him that, captivated by the delight they took in His divine face, in His words and in His manner, they forgot for whole days the food they needed.

  2. This holy modesty must accompany you at all times, by day and by night, taking care when you rest to be decently covered, and never to sleep without a shift; and in all places, even when you are alone, remember that you are in the presence of God and under my eyes. But you must take the greatest care to be modest in public actions: in the hospitals, with the sick in their homes, in the schools, etc. In these places be watchful that no distraction be seen in your eyes; that there be nothing soft or studied in your speech, nothing childish in your gestures, nothing affected in your walk.

  3. In your clothing you will not be slovenly, but you will guard well against excessive neatness, which might make whoever looks at you suspect that you have been at the mirror. You will not go out of your room unless decently dressed. It would be a fault greatly abhorred by me were I to see that among you, out of levity or in play, you touched one another’s hands, shoulders, etc. The custom among you shall be that, on leaving for distant places or on returning from them, you embrace one another as a sign of fraternal charity.

Detachment from Relatives

  1. My daughter, detachment from flesh and blood helps not a little in acquiring holy purity. You will therefore not have a disordered love for your relatives, remembering that Jesus does not want among the number of His disciples those who are not ready, for love of Him, to leave father, mother, brothers and sisters; and that, on the contrary, to whoever leaves them in order to follow Him He promises a hundredfold in this life and Paradise in the next. Listen, then, to my precepts on this detachment; by observing them you will honour the sacrifice I made when I offered my Daughter, still a little child, to the temple, leaving her there for the worship of her God.

  2. Whenever you receive visits from your relatives, even the very closest (except your father and mother), you will always receive them in the company of one of your fellow sisters assigned by the Superior, who will not leave for a moment as long as the visit lasts. It will never be permitted to do otherwise without the leave of the Superior, given expressly and not presumed.

  3. The Superior will not permit the sisters to receive visits from their relatives more than twice a year, unless some grave reason should call for greater latitude; it will be for her to examine this seriously.

  4. The Superior will not give leave to write to relatives more than once a year, unless some grave reason should require otherwise.

  5. During the visits you receive from your relatives, you will neither ask for nor receive anything; nor will you give them anything without the leave of the Superior.

  6. You will never invite the relatives who come to visit you unless, before making this invitation, you have first asked leave of your Superior.

  7. You will not show pleasure at being sent to a House of your Institute that is near your native place or your relatives.

  8. In your conversations you will take care never to bring in your relatives.

  9. When you write to them, you will never enter into discussion of their family affairs, e.g. marriages, lawsuits, business, employment, etc. And if in some case this should seem necessary to you for the glory of God and the good of their souls, then you will consult your Superior about it and abide by her counsel.

  10. You will never recommend your relatives, even those in the greatest need, to persons outside, so that they may obtain alms, or employment, etc., without first consulting your Superior.

  11. You will never visit your relatives, even if they live in the same city where you are stationed, and this is understood even in the case of grave and mortal illness; and this is understood also of your father and mother. This rule is of the greatest importance for maintaining the spirit among my daughters. Let the superiors know that a daughter of mine, going to her father’s house, would never return the same as she went, but would return greatly harmed in spirit. Let them therefore stand firm by it and not be quick to dispense from it. Strive then, my daughter, to keep your relatives far from your thoughts, for they distract greatly from union with God. Give yourself wholly to Jesus, and Jesus will take care of your own.

  12. My daughter, detachment from sensual pleasures, from flesh and blood, which I have urged upon you thus far, is far more effective for attaining my spirit than the detachment from earthly goods which the vow of holy Poverty makes you acquire. For your mind, freed from sense and from the flesh, like a heavenly vapour flies away to God by a living faith; your spirit neither hopes for nor tastes any delights but those dispensed by the hands of God; it esteems no person worthy of having its love, its friendship and its whole heart rest upon them, apart from its God. It no longer has any impulse to be double and feigning, since this impulse comes from the aim of acquiring some earthly delight or of fleeing some displeasure. Hence it is most simple. So too it is most prudent, for its eye, unsoiled by brutish earthly delight, is most luminous in discovering and following the ways that lead it to please its God. And it is also humble and meek, because in the very act of discovering the vileness of carnal delights, it sees too that it is at times tempted towards them, which humbles it greatly; and moreover, having trampled upon those pleasures which most brutalise those who abandon themselves to them, it remains full of humility and gentleness with all.

On the virtue of obedience, of which the Daughters of Saint Anne make a vow.

  1. My daughter, you know well that Jesus Christ was constituted by the Eternal Father Superior of all things; but He attained this supreme authority because He was the most subject and the most obedient to God. After Him, the highest authority was granted to my Daughter Mary, since she could command Jesus Christ her Son; but why did she have this supreme authority? Precisely because, after Jesus, she was the most obedient to her superiors. After Mary, I hold the supreme degree of authority, because I could command her, the true Mother of God. This, then, must be for you a sure sign that, after Mary and Jesus, there was no one in the world more subject and obedient to God than I.

My daughter, my Institute, to honour the obedience of Jesus, who obeyed even the wicked and went so far as to die in obedience to His Divine Father, and to honour that of Mary and my own, makes a vow of this virtue.

So that you may understand well to what obedience you bind yourself by this vow, know that in my Institute there is a supreme representative of mine, and this is the Superior General of the whole Institute; and it is to this Superior General that you make a vow of obedience. Now listen to the conditions which the obedience you owe her must have. 1st: you will obey her in all the things she commands you, provided that these things are not sin and, moreover, are in conformity with the Rules of the Institute; 2nd: your obedience to her must be prompt, cheerful and persevering; you must obey today, tomorrow and always; 3rd: it must be a blind obedience, which means that you obey without seeking the reason why you are commanded; and in this way you submit not only your will but also your judgement. This, however, does not forbid you, if the thing commanded or forbidden you should not, in your opinion, be suited to your spirit or proportioned to your strength, from making this known to your superiors; it is lawful for you to make this known, but with your spirit disposed, after you have made everything known, if the superiors do not accept your reasons, to go ahead and obey promptly; 4th: in order to obey you must not wait for the will of your superiors to be made known to you in the strict form of a command, such as: I command you, or I forbid you this; In virtue of holy obedience; I will, etc.; but it will suffice for you that it be disclosed to you in the gentle form of a request, such as: I would ask you to take up, or to leave, this office; it would be my intention; it would be good for you to do, or to leave, such a thing, etc.

  1. The Superior General has her lieutenants, and these are the Superiors whom she appoints to preside over the individual Houses of the Institute. To these she confers part of that full authority which she has over the whole Institute. Well then, to these Superiors, in the House where you are, you will render the obedience described in the preceding number, with which you are bound to obey the General. You must say the same if the General should appoint, besides the Superior, also an assistant Superior.

Hear, then, the whole order of Authority in my Institute. The Superiors receive their authority from the Superior General; the Superior General receives it from the Pope; and the Pope receives it from Jesus Christ; and so, my daughter, in obeying your Superior you obey the Pope, you obey Jesus Christ. All this is understood of the internal government of my Institute; for as regards its works for the neighbour, e.g. visits to the sick, service in the Hospitals, the education of girls in danger, etc., my Institute depends also on the Bishops in whose Dioceses it has Houses. You will obey also the sound of the bell, which is as the voice of your Superior when, at the various hours of the day, it calls you to the acts of piety, or other acts, laid down by the timetable. Your obedience to this sound will be so prompt that, if you are pen in hand, you leave the syllable you have begun; if you are speaking, you break off the word in your mouth at that very moment.

  1. To exercise yourself in this virtue of obedience, you will not perform any of those acts which are proper to the one who presides over the family, and which I indicate to you below.

  2. You will give no command, nor will you correct your sister for any fault, since these acts are proper to the one who is Superior. This is understood apart from the case in which the Superior has deputed you to perform one of these acts towards one of your fellow sisters. And if in your tasks you should need some help from your companion, you may ask her for it by way of a request. This, however, is understood to apply when the help is passing (it cannot be that a daughter of mine should have a quarter of an hour idle from her office); and if it should be for some length of time, before asking for it you will ask leave of the Superior.

  3. It is proper to the head of the family to keep up correspondence. Therefore you will not write any letter unless you have first asked leave of the Superior. Once you have written it, you will give it to the Superior, who will read it; and then it will be in her power to send it or to keep it back, as she thinks best, without your needing, my daughter, to know anything of it.

  4. So too, to teach or to have the members of the family taught is proper to the Head of the family. Therefore you may not teach a sister of yours to read and write, or to embroider, etc., without first asking the Superior’s leave for it. Likewise you may not ask to be instructed without first having asked leave of the Superior. Likewise you may not give anything in writing, not even a note, to a fellow sister without first asking leave of your Superior: much less is this lawful for you towards someone outside without that leave. And as you may not give, so you may not ask for anything in writing either from a fellow sister, and much less from a person outside, without that leave. All this must be understood when you do not hold an office that carries this leave with it.

  5. So too, it is the office of the one who stands at the head of the family to fix the hour for taking food; therefore it is not lawful for you to take food outside the time when the Community takes it, without the leave of the Superior.

  6. It is likewise an act of superiority to enter the rooms of the House and to bring others into them; hence you are forbidden to go to the room of your fellow sister, for any reason whatever, unless you have first asked leave of your Superior; and much less may you enter it without this leave when the Sister to whom it belongs is not inside. Having this leave, you will knock, and you will not enter until you have been told to come in. Likewise you are not permitted to invite a fellow sister to come into your room unless you have first obtained leave from the Superior. In all these cases, while they are together in the room conversing, they will leave its door somewhat open. This is understood unless the office you hold carries with it leave to do otherwise.

  7. The Head of the family, when he thinks fit, gathers his household to give them orders, and they must obey: so you will do; when the Superior gathers the House, you will hasten promptly, and at the time and place appointed for it you will listen in silence to what she has to say, and with respect and promptness you will carry it out.

  8. Since the lower Superior and the higher Superior form a single Superiority, when you receive from your Superior a refusal to any request of yours, you will not have recourse on the same matter to the higher Superior unless you disclose to her the refusal and the reasons given for it.

  9. When a Sister asks you to help her in some task, you will promptly lend yourself, provided that at that moment some more serious urgency does not prevent you, and provided that the help asked is passing and does not last more than a quarter of an hour; and if more time should be needed, you will not do it unless you have first asked leave of the Superior.

  10. Finally, you will punctually obey the timetable of the day, especially the hour of rising, of religious exercises, the hour for taking food, and for going to rest.

Behold, dear daughter, you have reached the midpoint of the detachment needed to clothe yourself with my spirit. As long as you had only freed your heart from earthly things, it could still stop at the delights of the flesh; freed also from the bonds of the flesh, there still remained to it one wretched refuge, namely that of its own will; but once released from this too, then there remains to it no creature on which to lean; it is happily constrained to seek all its rest in its God, to cling to His divine word by means of faith; to taste only the delights that flow from His divine bosom, by means of hope; to prize solely His divine greatness, His friendship, His union, by means of the virtue of charity. Then, esteeming only the majesty of its God, it lays aside all esteem of itself through holy humility. It no longer has anything of duplicity or pretence, either in speaking or in acting, which means that it is most simple; there is nothing any more that can make it angry; it is, in short, most prudent, never having the temptation to stray from its God. Behold, my daughter, how these three holy virtues of which you make a vow are like the body for which and in which live the seven virtues, Faith, Hope, Charity, Simplicity, Prudence, Humility and Meekness, which are its Spirit. Here it is that you possess all those parts which are necessary for you to offer that Sacrifice in the use of which you attain in a special way the immediate end of your vocation, which is to show yourself truly my daughter.

The Sacrifice is accomplished by means of the Spirit of the Love of God, which is its fire, and of the flesh, which is its matter, which must be consumed by the fire of Divine Love. The fire of Divine Love consumes the flesh in order to set it aflame and transform it into spirit, in the manner of which it is capable.

Observe all this in your Jesus on the cross: see how the fire of the Love of His Divine Father burns and consumes His divine flesh and makes it die, in order to make it wholly spiritual by means of His resurrection. So it is with you, my daughter, through the virtues of which I am speaking to you: the Spirit of Faith, Hope, Charity, Humility, Meekness is the fire of the Love of God, which, taking hold of your earthly things, of the delights of your flesh and of your will, envelops it [?] and, with the help of the three virtues of Poverty, Chastity and Obedience, consumes them and makes them die; so that the Heart thus remains wholly free to rest in its own sphere, that is, in the bosom of its God, and then, at the hour of the resurrection, to subject its flesh to itself and, as it were, change it into itself.

Now, my daughter, this sacrifice is the one that I, your Mother, offered every day of my life; and now I have made you my daughter in order to continue offering it in you, and with that same intention with which I myself offered it: namely, to thank my God for all His divine mercies and for all the graces He has bestowed on me, and above all for the greatest, which is that of having made me Mother of Mary Immaculate, who is His own Mother. See, then, how you can show me your filial love by observing these three holy vows of yours; but moved by the spirit of my love, which is wholly gathered up in the seven virtues that form the spirit of my Institute. All the acts of these three vows, as they are set down in their place, are so many hosts which, from morning to evening, you can offer to your God with the intention I have told you. Now you clearly understand that God has given me in all of you a people of Priestesses, who without ceasing offer Him sacrifice, to honour, praise, bless and thank Him until the end of the ages for having crowned me with the unique crown of Mother of the Immaculate. Respond, my daughter, to this most lofty vocation; be for me a holy Priestess on earth; and as your reward you will be one for all eternity in Heaven.

Charity towards the sick, of which the Daughters of Saint Anne make a vow.

  1. My daughter, so far I have spoken to you of those virtues which help you to acquire the Spirit of your vocation by detaching you from creatures: that is, of poverty, which detaches you from riches; of Chastity and its annexed virtues, modesty and detachment from relatives, which detach you from the pleasures of the flesh; and of obedience, which detaches you from yourself. Now I will speak to you of those virtues which you must practise in conversing in a holy manner with your neighbours; and first I will tell you how you must conduct yourself with those outside, and afterwards I will tell you how you must converse in a holy manner with your fellow sisters. First listen to the charity you must show to the sick.

My daughter, why ever did I merit to have so close a part in the redemption of the world as that of conceiving its Co-redemptrix, that is, my Immaculate Daughter Mary? Because my Heart was a sea of compassion for the spiritual and bodily miseries of my neighbours. In this I was a perfect portrait of Jesus Christ, for whom the work dearest to Him and most commended to His followers was the care of the sick. To draw us to this exercise of charity, the most repugnant to fallen nature, He assures us that He regards the care given to the sick as given to Himself. You, my daughter, are called to imitate me in this compassionate charity towards the sick, even to the point of making a vow of it. My daughter, now pay close attention to me, for I will teach you to what this vow binds you. You make a vow, then, to care for the sick whenever you are assigned to it by your superiors, and not otherwise; so that whenever your superiors assign you to care for the sick, you are then actually bound by your vow to this care; when you are not assigned to it, your vow does not then actually bind you to it.

  1. My daughter, what is the extent of this vow of yours? By virtue of your vow you can be assigned to the care of every kind of sick person, both in hospitals and in homes; to those sick with ordinary illnesses, and to those infected with any pestilence whatever, even when there is proximate danger that you may contract the same disease and fall victim to it; to care for them by day and by night. Now hear all my precepts on this virtue.

  2. You must regard yourself as the mother of the poor sick; you will love them with a maternal love; you will pray for them, and weep over their spiritual and temporal ills.

  3. Although you must nourish a lively desire to visit the sick and to serve them both in the hospitals and in their homes, yet you will never visit them without the express leave of your Superior. Likewise you will give them only such aid as is given to you by your Superior; and under pretext of charity you will never take anything to bring to them without the leave of the Superior.

  4. You will have a predilection for those sick who are abandoned by all, or who have very loathsome ailments, because in them you will recognise more clearly the passion of Jesus Christ.

  5. You will never go alone to visit the sick, but always in the company of a fellow sister. And if some case should require otherwise, it will be for the Superior to decide after serious reflection.

  6. On reaching the house of the sick person, you will ask to be taken to him at once, and you will not linger in conversation with the relatives, unless they should give you some information that would help you in caring for him well.

  7. On reaching the sick person’s bed, you will use the customary Christian greeting, that is: Praised be Jesus and Mary. Then, kneeling, you will say with your fellow sister a Pater noster to me, your Holy Mother; and if you have stayed some time, you will end the visit with this Pater noster.

  8. On reaching the sick person’s bed, you will at once recall the words of Jesus Christ, who says that He regards as done to Himself whatever good is done in His name to the sick; and at every service you render him you will keep saying in your Heart: Dear Jesus, I give You to eat, I give You to drink; dear Jesus, I dress Your wound, I make Your bed, etc.

  9. Knowing that when you stand before the sick person you are before Jesus, you will conduct yourself with humility and modesty; you will speak in a low voice; you will speak of things which at once relieve the sick person and edify those present. Be careful, however, not to wish to appear learned or too spiritual. To avoid this fault, the way is to speak little.

If you should notice that the Parish Priest is needed and that the relatives are not seeing to it, you will inform the Superior of this, so that she may see to it. If you see the need, you will exhort him with persuasive words to receive the Sacraments. If by chance you should be present at the death of the sick person and the Priest is absent, you will commend his soul. In this case, besides the most holy names of Jesus, Mary and Joseph, you will very often use my name, especially under the title of Mother of Mary Immaculate.

  1. If ever you should find some brutish sick person who, at the very moment you present yourselves to care for him, hurls insults at you, blasphemes the most holy name of God, of the Saviour and of His most holy Mother, you will not on that account leave him, nor lose heart; not even in those moments of diabolical fury will you rebuke him harshly; but you will strive to render him all the necessary services with great charity and assiduity; and meanwhile in your heart you will commend him to God, to Mary, and to me your Holy Mother. What if the sick person, at the sight of your charity in serving him for love of God, and your gentleness in speaking to him, moved by the grace of God, were to grow calm and be converted?…

  2. If the family is poor, you will inquire whether they carry out all the Doctor’s orders as regards the medicines, and if these are lacking because they are not buying them, you will inform the Superior, so that she may see to it. If you happen to be there at the time of the doctor’s visit, and the families are ignorant, you will remain present to hear the medicines he prescribes; if the family is educated and you notice that your presence makes them uneasy, you will withdraw with your companion to pray for as long as the visit lasts.

  3. You will take care not to give or suggest medicines on your own initiative, but you will keep to those prescribed by the Doctor. Likewise you will not talk about medicines, as though you wished to appear knowledgeable about them.

  4. If the sick person is of the other sex, you will take care not to feel his pulse; indeed, you will not readily feel it even for persons of the same sex, for in this there would be vanity. Likewise, when you must tend persons of the other sex, you will see to it that you do only what modesty permits.

  5. If, on arriving at the sick person’s, you should find there the priest assisting him, or if he should come while you are there, you will ask for his blessing, and for the whole time he remains there you will say no further word of a spiritual kind to the sick person.

  6. When you are with a sick person in a home, you will never separate from your companion; and when spending the night there, when one takes a little rest, she takes it under the eyes of her companion, who must keep watch during that time.

The Holy Mother. — My daughter, the care of the sick is a virtue of truly great price; for by this care you make a continual profession of faith that the Son of God became man, taking our flesh, and that in this flesh of ours He took all our infirmities, except sin, and that in it He was crucified and died to free us from all spiritual and temporal ills; all of which will come to pass in our glorious resurrection.

The daughter. — My Mother, ah! if in caring for the sick I had my Jesus continually present! How willingly I would bear everything in this care that is repugnant to nature!

The Holy Mother. — Dear one of my heart, hear a mystery: when you are caring for the sick, their Guardian Angels pay court to you, and you draw no breath, you take no step, but they carry all, all of it to Heaven to write it in the book of life. Hence at that time you have many Angels guarding you.

The daughter. — Then, my Mother, the hospitals, the rooms of the sick are for me a Paradise, where I converse with Jesus and with His Angels? What humility and reverence I need! How devoutly I must kiss the dust of those holy Houses of God!
